title: So, You Want to Work in Industry?
subtitle: Advice to colleagues who want to move from clinical practice to Industry
body_html:
When I started my career as a psychiatrist in 2011, the things I imagined doing with my time included:

  • Private practice

  • Working in a hospital

  • (maybe) doing some research.

Academic medicine is full of examples of people doing these three jobs. Working in the hospital could include a “wide” array of roles, from inpatient psychiatry attending to emergency psychiatry attending who sometimes covers the inpatient service. Oh, and time spent supervising residents while an inpatient or emergency psychiatry attending! There were even some ambitious doctors who began working in administration.

Note: for this article I will use “physician” referring to you, dear readers. I actually mean “health professional” or person who could be a company advisor, but I don't want to type so many words.

Since 2011, the range of options has gotten broader. This is true for me and for anyone else going through training. It’s even true for those plotting their escape from academia now. Many of the young—and even older—psychiatrists I connect with look at my career path and imagine intention and planning. This is not entirely true, but I have learned a few things along the way.

What Kind of Companies Count As “Industry?”

First, I will take a swing at defining “industry” to frame our discussion in this article, and then provide practical advice on how to take the first steps towards considering those careers. The major industrial careers for brain medicine professionals (I'm including psychiatrists, and other licensed health professionals who could be doing clinical work, but might not want to) are roughly broken up into:

  1. “Life Sciences” — these are the companies building the drugs and devices that we use to treat our patients in clinical medicine.

    1. Traditional Pharma: giants such as Otsuka, Bristol Myers Squibb, and Johnson & Johnson, among others. These companies have massive marketing budgets, large clinical trial budgets, and market capitalizations in the billions of dollars. They are often publicly traded organizations, operating on a global scale.

    2. Early-Stage Pharma: These companies are developing medicines that are still in the early stages of development. Some of them may already be publicly traded, but they have a fraction of the budgets the big players do.

    3. Medical Device: medical advice; companies tend to be smaller, with a few exceptions (e.g., Medtronic), and have a more complex “go-to-market” for their devices than pharma does for drugs.

    4. Contract research organizations — these are the entities that run clinical trials for the above drug and device companies.

    5. Consulting, Software, Regulatory, Media, Marketing: all of the above companies need support from software vendors and consultants who make their work possible. These include law firms, Ex-industry pros, marketing agencies, conference hosts, and industry publications—like this one, sometimes.

  2. Payors: all of our massive insurance companies hire doctors and other health professionals at various levels. There are executives all the way down to peons, but these are huge companies with massive budgets.

    1. Myriad companies support the major payor ecosystem, and “smaller” health plans like those managed by self-funded employers— physicians often work in these companies, too.

  3. Health tech companies1

    1. These companies are mostly startups, although a few have exited public markets, such as TalkSpace, Lifestance, and others. Overwhelmingly, these companies promise that they'll use technology to make the experience of getting care better or more accessible, and they are trying to scale, overwhelmingly by working with big insurance.

      Many of these companies have substantial budgets, but they're not profitable most of the time—they raised venture capital to fund a competitive advantage in their theoretically proprietary technology. They sometimes make software for other healthcare players. The best known of these companies is Epic—the hospital software leviathan. This podcast is mandatory listening:

      You can mentally divide these companies into two buckets: those that directly make money by providing healthcare, and those that sell services that are not healthcare.

What Owen Scott Muir, M.D., is Doing… Now

Most readers probably know that your Editor-in-Chief here at The Frontier Psychiatrists has two current jobs:

I’m a co-founder and Chief Medical Officer of Radial, a health-technology and services company that provides next-generation Brain Medicine as the standard of care to our patients.

I’m also the Chief Medical Officer at Neurolief. This medical technology company built Relivion MG for Migraine and now ProLivᵀᴹ Rx for Depression, which hasn’t responded to first-line treatment (MOOD study pre-print published here).

Join the waitlist for the (imminent) device launch here.

This at-home and in-clinic device was FDA Approved at the end of last year. Here is the label:

The Proliv™Rx System provides focal external Combined Occipital and Trigeminal Afferent Stimulation (eCOT-AS) treatment. It is intended as an adjunctive treatment for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) in adults who failed to achieve satisfactory improvement from at least one previous antidepressant medication, for use at home or in clinic. It is a prescription-only device.

I dig into that technology and others like it here. A nice review of neuromodulation, broadly, which is straightforward is here.

It does seem like I do a lot of work. However, is that I didn’t just go from zero to CMO of multiple companies after I tripped over an opportunity and fell, by chance into the roles. There were steps I took to get there, and this article breaks them down for you.

Recommended First Steps, and “Easy” Wins

As a future senior executive, you need to be an expert at something. It’s ideal if you are an expert at many things, but the one area in which real expertise is useful in being a good doctor. You know, with patients. There is only one tried and true way to get great at seeing patients—which is to see a lot of them. If you are a resident, it means extra moonlighting. If you are an early career doctor, it probably means moonlighting. But you should probably see a lot of patients per unit time in the first few years of your career. I did an extra shifts every 3rd night or weekend day of my 4th year of residency—you don’t have to do more than is wise for you however. A simple rule is to work one more moonlighting shift per month that would be “a breeze” for you. Push your self, a little, but not to the point of burnout.

Some of this experience should be outpatient, because that is more likely to be where innovative companies will bring their products to market. Maybe you spend some time in hospital settings too, so you know how that works, too?

Try to make a positive change in your hospital setting. See how hard it is. Take notes. Make friends. Be helpful. Those little favors you do? Getting lunch for a junior resident, taking an extra shift to cover for your supervisor? It all makes your ability to hire anyone you would want on your team easier in the future. Every coworker should be a future “hire” in your mind, if you respect them, and they respect you. It barely matters what roles you are in at the time when you first meet. Make a great impression! Great teams come together more quickly if you have worked together before—just ask Costco.

Some of the Companies I Advise, and Examples of Why I Worked With Them.

After you have being a good doctor under your belt, the next step is becoming an advisor. Jumping ship from practice to industry entirely is a major leap, and you want to have some ability to know if the job you are taking is likely to be the best possible fit for you. This means doing some dating, by advising companies you are curious about to make connections, built some pattern recognition, and have some experience with the very different pace of industry vs. academics.

These roles are often compensated in a mix of cash and/or equity. There is a standard contract for startups, called the FAST. You will see it more than once. Standard documents make diligence in fundraising easier, and that is in your interest once you have an equity stake in a company.

Having some equity (usually In the form of “stock options”) aligns your efforts with the success of the company2.

Here are some of my formal advisory gigs, with backstory. I was originally going to do them all in this one article, and then realized I’d never finish it if I did that. So, I chose some examples instead.

Advisory Vignettes

Senior Medical Advisor, Ampa Health

I am thrilled to be an advisor to AMPA, which is working on the most scalable TMS technology I’ve seen to date. Both Carlene (my wife) and I are advisors to Ampa. For one thing—and this is the most important part—we really like the team, personally. And startup is more likely to be worth nothing than something by the time there is a “liquidity event.” Ampa wanted us as advisors cause we are great, of course. For me, I adore and respect Jonathan Downar, Don, and everyone else there. It’s a LTR as an advisor—you aren't spending all day with companies when you aren’t working there, but you will work together over years to decades before any money for anything. The most important question to answer is—if this financially goes no where, will it still be time well spent?

If yes, you are in a good spot!

If it seems like it will be a lof of work, and you would rather get paid money? That is usually a consulting gig. Those are fine too, but it’s not as alighted with the long term success of the company, and there is no big pay day at the end—or profound sadness when the company folds.

Medical Advisor, Purple Gaze.io

This is an awesome company, based in Utrecht, Netherlands, that makes next generation eye tracking hardware and software. We can read minds (maybe) but watching someones eyes move around faster than our traditional cameras can pick up—or than our brains can consciously register. They approached me, I met the team, reviewed the data, and said yes. Being able to quickly review data—a skill you built in clinical practice—is the ability to decide is a gig is worth your time!

Strategic Advisor, Graymatters Health

Based in Tel Aviv, Israel, Graymatters Health makes the PRISM system. The CEO, Oded Kraft, has been to my home for dinner, because he’s a great dinner guest—not only because we work together. This relationship started when my clinc became an early customer of the PRISM Suite. I had feedback on the product, and how to get other clinicians to incorporate it into their practice, and lo and behold, they offered an advisory role. Did it make sense for me to do? Yes—because I wanted them to listen to me anyway!

People I'd spend my time with anyway? Check. Work I'd probably be doing anyway? Check. Something I'm proud to advocate for regardless of any incentive? Check.

Working as an advisor, doesn't feel like work if you already want to champion the success of whatever it is!

Strategic Advisor, Spring Health

This was a consulting arrangement, I don't have any equity, but I really like them. I think their go-to-market first in the self-funded employer market is smart. Most crucially, I like Dr. Mill Brown, their CMO, and he’s fun to work with. So, I said yes, and I am proud of my contribution.

Strategic Advisor, Psyrin

I've been obsessed with vocal bio markers for a long time. Psyrin was doing the best work I've ever seen with vocal biomarkers. I had opinions, they had time to hear them. My team ended up running a clinical trial with Psyrin, and I want to see them succeed. Thus, people I'd spend time with anyway? Check. On a mission I am aligned with? You get the point. For prior writing about what they're up to, feel free to check out this interview.

In Summary: Align on People, and Possibility

Working in industry is not for everyone. Startups? Even less of a sure thing. If you are considering making the jump from clinical work to industry, you need to ask yourself a few key questions:

  1. Do I love the people I will be working with?

  2. Will I make more of an impact, and maybe even more money (possibly) doing this plausibly riskier thing?

  3. Am I risk tolerant, and thus can work at an earlier stage company, which is like a job with a lottery ticket attached?

  4. Am I risk averse, in which case industry jobs should pay me enough (both in money/other sure-fire compensation and benefit to the world) to make up for forsaking the known benefit and pay of healing humans in my day job?

I think working for the greater good is fun—but it’s a gamble. Every patient I’d see will get the benefit of my training. In industry, it might pay off big, but it’s more of a gamble. As physicians, we’d make the most money never practicing medicine, so that isn’t the real driver for most of us as to how we chose to spend out time. But if we want to make a big impact, there is always the chance that it won’t work out. Thus, make sure you love the people you are working with, and find the work invigorating.

Good luck, colleagues. Let’s all change the world, a little bit.
